source: Morpheme Matrices, Marn Frank, ATLAS/Hamline University (expanded March 2018), p.6-31
extraction_notes: matrices.json covers Matrix 1-18 (Latin roots, p.6-23) and Matrix 19-25 (Greek forms, p.25-31); the blank template matrix on p.32 is a teacher worksheet with no content and is not included.

'prefixes.common' / 'suffixes.derivational' reproduce each matrix's own printed lists (not the full top-10 charts). 'prefixes.less_common' captures the smaller secondary prefix box shown in some Latin matrices, or (for Greek matrices) the left-column Greek forms, which function like prefixes in that position of the matrix.

In Matrix 18 the source text lists 'expounder' twice ('expounds, expounder, expounding, expounder') where every parallel word family in that matrix follows an -s/-ed/-ing/-er pattern (impounds/impounded/impounding/impounder, compounds/compounded/compounding/compounder). The first 'expounder' was corrected to 'expounded' by that pattern; flagged here rather than silently invented.

Several Word Key entries marked '(plus ...)' in the source are bonus words that use forms not in that matrix's own prefix/left-form list (e.g. Matrix 22's homophone/megaphone/vibraphone/xylophone use homo-/mega-/vibra-/xylo-, none of which are in Matrix 22's own left column). These bonus words are kept in example_words and word-key.json with best-effort morpheme splits, but their extra forms are not added to prefixes.json/greek-forms.json since they do not appear in any matrix diagram itself.

Matrix 20's Word Key pairs the left form 'meter' (measure) with 'logy' to produce 'meteorology/meteorologic/meteorological' - these are the ordinary English weather-science words (from Greek 'meteoros'), not a clean meter+logy concatenation; kept as printed, morphemes split as meteor+logy(+ic+al) for legibility.

matrices.teaching_notes: Latin-root matrix (root form, to shape, free). Follow the source's 8 explicit instruction steps for Latin-root matrices (p.6): explain why bigger/longer words matter; model pronunciation and meaning of the root; assemble root+suffixes first when the root is free; model prefixes from the p.3 chart; assemble prefix+root; then model/guide prefix+root+suffix combinations, checking the Word Key; guide rereading, spelling, and oral sentence use; have students write A Few Sentences.

Follow the source's 8 explicit instruction steps for Latin-root matrices (p.6): explain why bigger/longer words matter; model pronunciation and meaning of the root; assemble root+suffixes first when the root is free; model prefixes from the p.3 chart; assemble prefix+root; then model/guide prefix+root+suffix combinations, checking the Word Key; guide rereading, spelling, and oral sentence use; have students write A Few Sentences. Source text repeats 'expounder' twice in place of the expected 'expounds, expounded, expounding, expounder' pattern; corrected here to 'expounded' by analogy with 'impounded/compounded' (flagged in extraction_notes).

Greek-form matrix (root gram, graph, written or drawn). Follow the source's 8 explicit instruction steps for Greek-form matrices (p.25): explain that subjects like science, geography, or civics use big Greek-based words; review the Greek sound patterns ph=/f/, ch=/k/, y=short/long i; model the middle Greek form and its meaning; model the left-column Greek forms; combine left forms with the middle form into subject words, checking the Word Key; when ready, add the derivational suffixes; guide rereading, spelling, and oral sentence use; have students write A Few Sentences. Inflectional suffixes (-s/es, -ed, -ing) are intentionally omitted from Greek-form matrices.

Inflectional suffixes (-s/es, -ed, -ing) are intentionally omitted from Greek-form matrices. 'meteorology/-logic/-logical' pair the left form 'meter' (measure) with 'logy' in the source, but the word actually reflects the unrelated English word 'meteor'; split shown here as meteor+logy for readability, flagged in extraction_notes.
